title: Listen to a Conversation
lines: In this task you hear a short conversation between two people, usually students, a student and a staff member, or friends in an everyday setting. Each conversation is about 80-150 words long with 6-10 turns, and it is followed by two questions.
## What is on the screen
- While you listen, the screen may show a simple picture of the setting or the speakers. The questions do not appear until the conversation ends.
- After the audio, two multiple-choice questions appear, one at a time, with four options each.
- You hear the conversation once only. You may take notes.
## Timing

Listening lasts about 29 minutes in total, in two adaptive stages. A conversation takes under a minute to hear; then you have a short time for each question. Keep moving: you cannot go back to earlier questions after the next recording starts.
## What is being tested
- The gist: why the people are talking and what the main topic is.
- Key details: a time, a reason, a change of plan, a problem.
- A speaker's purpose or attitude: is she pleased, worried, unsure, surprised?
- What will happen next: the final decision or plan.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: The first two turns usually show the reason for the conversation. Listen hard at the start: "I'm here because ...", "Do you have a minute? I wanted to ask about ...".
- Step 2: Take short notes in two columns, one for each speaker. Write key words only: problem, reason, suggestion, decision.
- Step 3: Listen for changes in direction: "Actually ...", "Oh, but ...", "The thing is ...", "In that case ...". The answer often comes right after such words.
- Step 4: Listen for tone. "Oh, great" can be real pleasure or disappointment, depending on the voice and the context.
- Step 5: The last turns usually give the plan. Questions about what will happen next are answered there.
- Step 6: When the questions come, answer the gist question from your overall understanding, and detail questions from your notes.
## Worked example 1
> Woman (student): Hi, I'm trying to register for the advanced photography class, but the system says it's full.
> Man (office assistant): Let me see. Yes, all twenty places are taken. There is a waiting list, though.
> Woman: How long is it?
> Man: Only three names right now. People often drop the class in the first week, so you have a good chance.
> Woman: Okay. I'd rather not wait without a backup, though. Is there anything similar?
> Man: There's a digital imaging course on Tuesday evenings. It covers editing more than shooting.
> Woman: That might work. Can I join the waiting list and register for the evening course too?
> Man: Sure, and if a photography place opens, you can switch.
> Question 1: Why does the woman go to the office?
> A. To complain about the photography teacher
> B. To get help with a class that has no places left
> C. To drop the digital imaging course
> D. To buy equipment for a photography class
B, from her first turn. The answer paraphrases "the system says it's full" as "no places left". D and A are not mentioned; C reverses her plan.
> Question 2: What will the woman probably do?
> A. Wait for the first week of classes before deciding
> B. Take only the digital imaging course
> C. Join the waiting list and sign up for a second course
> D. Ask the teacher to add a twenty-first place
C repeats her final plan in new words. A is what she says she would rather not do. B ignores the waiting list.
## Worked example 2
> Man: Amara, did you finish the slides for our presentation?
> Woman: Most of them. I'm stuck on the chart for the survey results.
> Man: Oh, I can do that part. I made one for my economics class last week.
> Woman: Really? That would save me hours. But you're already writing the conclusion.
> Man: The conclusion's almost done. Send me the numbers tonight.
> Woman: You're a lifesaver. I'll email them as soon as I get home.
> Question: What does the woman mean when she says "You're a lifesaver"?
> A. She thinks the man works in a hospital.
> B. She is very grateful for his help.
> C. She is worried about his safety.
> D. She wants him to give the presentation.
B. "Lifesaver" is an idiom for someone who helps at an important moment. A and C take the words literally.
## What good notes look like
For worked example 1, useful notes take ten seconds to write and are enough to answer both questions:
> W: photo class full
> M: wait list, 3 names, drop wk 1
> W: backup? -> digital imaging, Tue eve
> PLAN: wait list + eve course, switch later
Notice that the notes capture the problem, the suggestions and the final plan, not every word.
## Common traps
- Options that repeat words from the conversation but change who did what.
- A suggestion that was made and rejected, presented as the final decision.
- Details that are true but do not answer the gist question.
- Literal readings of idioms ("lifesaver", "on the same page", "running behind").
- Missing the change of plan that comes after "actually" or "but".
! Many next-action questions are answered in the last two turns. Keep your attention until the very end of the recording.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to everyday conversations in English: campus videos, learner podcasts, TV series about students or offices. After each scene, say who talked, why, and what they decided.
- Practise note-taking with symbols: arrows for change, a check for agreement, a question mark for uncertainty.
- Learn common conversational idioms and phrases for suggestions, agreement and refusal.
- Practise listening once only. Do not pause or replay in practice sets; review the script only after you answer.
